summaries.Q159884: At the Foro Italico, a first stadium came out of the sports complex project entrusted in 1928 to Enrico Del Debbio, the Stadio dei Cipressi. After the Second World War, the Italian Olympic committee asked Annibale Vitellozzi to build a large stadium there, opened on 17 May 1953. Lazio and AS Roma play their matches there.
summaries.Q162353: Built in 203 to glorify the victories of Septimius Severus and his sons Caracalla and Geta over the Parthians, this marble arch has a main archway flanked by two smaller ones. Caracalla murdered Geta in 212, then had his brother's name in the dedication replaced by further titles.
summaries.Q213678: The state library of the Holy See, it grew from the holdings Nicholas V began gathering around 1450, when the Vatican collection numbered 340 ancient manuscripts; at the pope's death it held 1,200. Sixtus IV made it an institution in 1475. Access is limited to researchers holding a doctorate.
summaries.Q848386: Commissioned by cardinal Alessandro Farnese, the future pope Paul III, this High Renaissance palace drew on the most important architects of the day, over some 75 years of work: Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, Michelangelo, Vignola, then Giacomo della Porta, who finished it in 1589. The French embassy has been there since 1874.
summaries.Q12512: The largest Catholic church in the world, it stands on the site of the ancient Vatican basilica. Julius II had its first stone laid on 18 April 1506 and it was finished in 1626. Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno and Bernini are among its architects. It is the pope's church, not the cathedral of Rome.
summaries.Q849241: A small Ionic temple in the forum Boarium, dedicated to Portunus, Roman god of harbours, close to the portus Tiberinus, the first river port of Rome. Other dedications were long ascribed to it, among them Fortuna Virilis. Its conversion into a church in the Middle Ages saved it from destruction.
summaries.Q2932918: A historic bar on the square of the same name, in the rione of Sant'Eustachio, founded in 1938 in the premises of a former coffee roaster. Arabica beans from South America are roasted there over a wood fire, in a machine dating from 1948. Romans rate it one of the best espressos in the capital.
summaries.Q63785: Rectangular and lined with historic palaces, it takes its name from the Column of Marcus Aurelius, which has stood there since antiquity and also gave its name to the rione Colonna. Laid out in the late 16th century at the initiative of pope Sixtus V, it has a fountain made in 1577 to a design by Giacomo Della Porta.
summaries.Q728399: Film studios founded in 1937 in the Don Bosco district, wanted by the fascist government to rival Hollywood and serve propaganda. Mussolini laid the first stone in 1936. A German concentration camp from 1943 to 1944, the site held a displaced persons camp from 1945 to 1947, then revived with American shoots.
summaries.Q281330: The first complete wall around Rome, begun under the monarchy, it bears the name of Servius Tullius but was almost entirely rebuilt in the 4th century BC, after the sack of the city by the Gauls in 390. About 10 m high, it lost its defensive role under the Empire; a 94 m stretch survives in front of Rome Termini station.
summaries.Q182955: Twelve museums, five galleries and one thousand four hundred rooms hold the collection gathered over centuries by the popes: about 70,000 works, 20,000 of them on show. It goes back to the early 16th century, when Julius II had ancient statues installed in the Belvedere gardens. It was the second most visited museum in the world in 2024.
summaries.Q1362663: Built around 1564 for cardinal Giovanni Ricci di Montepulciano on the Pincio, it passed in 1576 to cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici, who fitted it out for his art collection and gave the seven hectare park an Italian garden. Galileo stayed there six months under house arrest in 1633. It has housed the Academy of France since 1803.
summaries.Q2943: The main chapel of the apostolic palace, dedicated to the Assumption of Mary, it takes its name from pope Sixtus IV and was consecrated in 1483. Its walls carry frescoes by Botticelli and Perugino; Michelangelo painted the vault from 1508 to 1512, then the Last Judgment around 1535-1541. Cardinals in conclave elect the pope there.
summaries.Q752555: Raised in 141 by Senate decree by Antoninus Pius for his deified wife Faustina, it was dedicated a second time to both spouses after the emperor's death in 161. Its cella has held the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda since the early Middle Ages, hence its good preservation: the pronaos columns, 17 m high, are all in place.
summaries.Q1050350: Built by the impresario Domenico Costanzi to plans by Achille Sfondrini, it opened on 27 November 1880 as the Teatro Costanzi. Placed in 1888 under the publisher Sonzogno, it opened to young composers and saw the premieres of Cavalleria rusticana and Tosca. Renamed Teatro Reale dell'Opera in 1928, it took its present name in 1946.
summaries.Q1202365: A circular square near Termini station, it was called piazza Esedra until 1960, after the exedra of the Roman baths; that name is still used locally. The Fountain of the Naiads stands at its centre: its unveiling in 1901 gave rise to a masquerade, the last notable event of the Carnival of Rome.
summaries.Q2329591: The official seat of the Sovereign Order of Malta, on via Condotti, it belongs to the Order and is granted extraterritorial status by the Italian government. Left in 1629 by Antonio Bosio, it was first the seat of the Order's ambassador to the Papal States, before becoming in 1834 the residence of the Grand Master.
summaries.Q216568: A group of large squares bordering the Roman Forum to the north east, built between 54 BC and AD 113, when the old forum became too cramped. Julius Caesar first, then Augustus, Vespasian, Domitian and Trajan, each had a vast enclosed square laid out there for his political programme. Trajan's forum, the last, is the largest.
summaries.Q486382: Begun in 118 as Hadrian's mausoleum and finished under Antoninus Pius in 139, it was taken into the Aurelian Wall in 403 and became a fortress. Its name comes from the vision of the archangel Michael credited to Gregory I during the plague of 590. A papal refuge, it was a prison until 1901 and has held a museum since 1906.
summaries.Q2047548: Seat of the presidency of the Italian Council of Ministers since 1961, it runs along the Via del Corso and has its main entrance on the Piazza Colonna. Its story begins in 1578, when the Aldobrandini family brought together and reworked several properties facing the square. The Chigi handed it to the Italian state in 1916.
summaries.Q84090: The cathedral of the bishop of Rome and the first monumental Christian building put up in the West, it carries on its pediment the title of mother and head of all the churches of the City and the world. More than 250 councils have been held there. Borromini reworked the nave for the 1650 jubilee, Alessandro Galilei the travertine facade in 1735.
summaries.Q1229008: On the Pincio, at the top of the steps above piazza di Spagna, this French national church was consecrated in 1585 by Sixtus V. Its crossing vault, in late French Gothic style, is the only example of its kind in Rome. In front of it stands an obelisk from the gardens of Sallust, raised on the orders of Pius VI in 1788.
summaries.Q588377: Opened on 31 January 1732 with Domenico Sarro's opera Berenice, it was built by the Cesarini family out of their town house. Foreign visitors in the 18th century held it to be the most important of the Roman theatres. Rossini premiered the Barbiere di Siviglia there in 1816. The hall houses the Teatro di Roma foundation.
summaries.Q1140395: Cut through between 1936 and 1950 under Mussolini's government by demolishing the spina of the Borgo, it links Castel Sant'Angelo to piazza Pio XII, which opens onto St Peter's Square. Its name recalls the Lateran Accords of 1929. Straight and over 420 metres long, it cancels the baroque perspective devised by Bernini.
summaries.Q2047551: Also called palazzo dei Penitenzieri, this palace on the Via della Conciliazione, in the Borgo, was begun around 1480 for cardinal Domenico della Rovere to plans by Baccio Pontelli. Its facade takes up the style of the Palazzo Venezia. Excavations in its courtyard from 2020 have brought to light the theatre of Nero.
summaries.Q746102: The main collecting sewer of ancient Rome, this channel takes the water of the valleys between the Quirinal and the Esquiline, crosses the Roman Forum and empties into the Tiber. Tradition dates the start of the works to around 600 BC. Open at first, it was gradually covered. Its conduits still drain the Foro Romano.
summaries.Q841506: A public museum housed in a villa built for the Borghese from 1607 by Flaminio Ponzio, the work then passing to Giovanni Vasanzio. Part of cardinal Scipione Borghese's collection was moved there as early as March 1613. The Italian state bought the villa and its collections in 1902; the gallery reopened after restoration in June 1997.
summaries.Q1123879: Built between 1455 and 1467 for the Venetian cardinal Pietro Barbo, the future pope Paul II, it was in turn a papal residence and the embassy of the republic of Venice, hence its name. Mussolini made it the seat of government and his private apartment, and addressed crowds from its balcony. It holds the Palazzo Venezia national museum.
summaries.Q186282: Built at the top of the Esquiline, it is one of Rome's four major basilicas and one of the first churches raised in honour of the Virgin Mary. Sixtus III consecrated it on 5 August 434. The only basilica in Rome to have kept its original early Christian structure, it preserves the mosaics of the nave and of the triumphal arch.
summaries.Q586468: The main place of worship of ancient Roman religion, it crowned the Capitoline Hill and was dedicated to the Capitoline triad: Jupiter in the centre, Juno on the left, Minerva on the right. Military triumphs ended there with a sacrifice. Burnt down several times, it was each time rebuilt more lavishly.
summaries.Q2291009: A small roofed theatre for musical performances, in imitation of Greek odeons, it stood on the Campus Martius, immediately south of the stadium of Domitian, and could hold 10,000 spectators. The facade of the Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne, founded on its cavea, keeps its curved shape.
summaries.Q34921: A monumental square at the top of the Capitoline Hill, it stands on the Asylum, the dip between the Arx and the Capitolium; the Cordonata capitolina leads up to it. Paul III entrusted its renovation to Michelangelo, who accentuated the turning of the hill towards St Peter's Basilica. The council of Rome sits there.
summaries.Q2901320: On the second floor of the Oratory of the Filippini, on piazza della Chiesa Nuova, in the rione of Parione, it takes its name from the nearby church of Santa Maria in Vallicella. The building was designed by Francesco Borromini for the Congregation of the Oratory. The collection originally came from Philip Neri's own library.
summaries.Q622438: Built for Nero from the year 65, after the fire of Rome, it took its name from the gold leaf of its decoration and covered several dozen hectares: separate buildings, gardens, an artificial lake, a revolving banquet hall. After 69 the space was given back to the Roman public and Vespasian raised the Flavian amphitheatre on the drained lake.
summaries.Q333906: Created in 1471 by Sixtus IV to hold ancient bronzes given to the Roman people, among them the Capitoline Wolf, they pass for the first museum in the world and opened to the public in 1734 under Clement XII. Benedict XIV added the Capitoline picture gallery. Their historic seat is the Palazzo Nuovo and the Palazzo dei Conservatori.
summaries.Q781417: Designed by Bernini for cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi, it was unfinished at the death of pope Gregory XV in 1623; work resumed under Innocent X, with Carlo Fontana altering the plans. The apostolic Curia moved in in 1696. Made the seat of the Chamber of Deputies after 1870, it was rebuilt by Ernesto Basile, the front facade excepted.
summaries.Q231699: One of Rome's four major basilicas, it was raised by Constantine over the necropolis holding the tomb of Saint Paul, outside the Aurelian Wall. Levelled then rebuilt much larger from 386, it burnt in 1823; the apse, the transept and the cloister were spared. The rebuilding, begun in 1825, kept the early Christian plan.
summaries.Q569253: Laid out by Michelangelo in the central hall of the Baths of Diocletian, by order of pope Pius IV and at the request of the Sicilian priest Antonio del Duca, it also occupies the former caldarium and tepidarium rooms. Luigi Vanvitelli decorated the interior from 1749. It is used for national ceremonies.
summaries.Q3687231: A music school in central Rome, it comes under the national academy of Saint Cecilia and took its present form in 1875, at the urging of Giovanni Sgambati and Ettore Pinelli. The body it derives from, the Congregazione dei Musici di Roma, an Accademia from 1585, was first led by Palestrina. Ennio Morricone studied there.
summaries.Q616887: One of the gates of the Servian Wall, on the Esquiline, near where the via Labicana meets the via Tiburtina. Under Augustus it was rebuilt as a triple bay triumphal arch, still visible, dedicated in 262 to the emperor Gallienus by Marcus Aurelius Victor. The church of Santi Vito e Modesto, rebuilt in 1477, backs onto it.
summaries.Q10285: Oval, between the Esquiline and the Caelian, it is the largest amphitheatre built in the Roman Empire. Work began between 70 and 72 under Vespasian and ended in 80 under Titus; Domitian added a gallery at the top and created the hypogeum. In use for nearly five centuries, it held animal and gladiator fights and executions.
summaries.Q369075: It is the last monument raised in the Roman Forum. Corinthian, with a fluted shaft, the column stands nearly 13.6 metres. The exarch of Ravenna Smaragdus set it on the rostra on 1 August 608 to carry a statue of the Byzantine emperor Phocas, in thanks for his policy favourable to the bishops of Rome.
summaries.Q623612: Augustus raised this altar to Pax, goddess of Peace, between 13 and 9 BC, by decision of the Senate after his return from Gaul and Spain, in the northern part of the Campus Martius. Buried by Tiber floods, found again in the 16th century, it was reassembled in 1937-1938 near the mausoleum of Augustus, in a pavilion opened by Mussolini.
summaries.Q2031943: Begun in the late 15th century at the initiative of cardinal Riario, finished in 1513, it was seized by the newly elected pope Leo X, then became in 1517 the seat of the Apostolic Chancery. The tribunals of the Roman Curia still sit there and the building remains Vatican property. The Sala dei Cento Giorni has frescoes by Vasari.
summaries.Q542070: This minor basilica in the rione of Monti was built between 432 and 440 on foundations of the Roman Republic, to hold the chains of Saint Peter imprisoned in Jerusalem, venerated as relics. The right transept holds the tomb of Julius II, commissioned from Michelangelo in 1505 and finished only in 1545; the Moses is at its centre.
summaries.Q1133288: The Roman Forum received this temple to the deified Julius Caesar. Shortly after the murder, a column and an altar had been set up where the pyre stood, but Dolabella had them destroyed at the end of April 44 BC. The Senate ordered the temple on their site in 42, and Octavian dedicated it on 18 August 29 BC.
summaries.Q1109934: It is the oldest working theatre in Rome, built in wood for the private use of Camillo Capranica and opened on 7 January 1727. The 1791 works having kept the wood, government architects required its rebuilding in stone, completed by Gaspare Salvi in 1822. In 2011 it closed, then was occupied by entertainment workers.
summaries.Q1541068: This vast rectangular square on the Campus Martius, on the corso Vittorio Emanuele, is almost entirely taken up by a sacred area of four republican temples, labelled A, B, C and D for lack of certainty about the gods honoured. Behind temples B and C survives the base of the Curia of Pompey, where Caesar was murdered.
summaries.Q99309: On the piazza della Rotonda, this temple built on Agrippa's orders was first dedicated to all the Roman gods. Damaged by several fires, it was entirely rebuilt under Hadrian, then turned into a church in the 7th century by pope Boniface IV. Its dome, the largest of antiquity, reaches 43.30 m in internal diameter.
summaries.Q1127325: This Roman bridge crosses the Tiber 3 km from the historic centre, where the via Flaminia and the via Cassia met to cross the river. In October 312 it gave its name to the battle between Constantine and his rival Maxentius. Partly destroyed in 1849 by Garibaldi's troops then restored, it has been pedestrian only since 1978.
summaries.Q1126723: Baldassarre Peruzzi built this suburban villa from 1508, in the rione of Trastevere, for the Sienese banker Agostino Chigi, treasurer to pope Julius II. It received frescoes by Peruzzi, by Raphael and his school, by Sebastiano del Piombo and by Sodoma. Cardinal Alessandro Farnese bought it around 1580 and gave it its name.
summaries.Q64103: On the Capitoline square, the building was the seat of the Conservators, the elected magistracy that governed lay Rome. Michelangelo designed its facade, finished after his death by Giacomo della Porta in 1568. The Treaty of Rome was signed there in 1957. With the Palazzo Nuovo and the Tabularium it now forms the Capitoline Museums site.
summaries.Q719794: The mother church of the Society of Jesus, built from 1568 to plans by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola and funded by cardinal Alessandro Farnese, it was consecrated in 1584. Giacomo della Porta built the facade from 1575 and designed the dome. Giovanni Battista Gaulli painted the vault in trompe-l'oeil between 1672 and 1683.
summaries.Q430792: The largest temple of ancient Rome by area was begun in 121, under Hadrian, between the old Roman Forum and the Colosseum, on ground held by the vestibule of the Domus aurea; the colossus of Nero had to be moved. The building set back to back two cellae, dedicated to Venus Felix and to Roma Aeterna.
summaries.Q18708327: Raised in 1718 by Antonio D'Alibert as the Teatro Alibert, this lost theatre was auctioned after its founder went bankrupt, then bought and renamed by Roman nobles. As long as women were not allowed to perform in the Papal States, castrati took the female roles. A fire destroyed it in 1863.
summaries.Q1632777: A gate of the Servian Wall, it stood on the south west slopes of the Caelian, near the sacred grove of the Camenae where the Appian Way starts, and gave its name to the first of the fourteen regions into which Augustus divided Rome in 7 BC. Remains were uncovered in 1867. The piazza di Porta Capena occupies its site.
summaries.Q180212: Between the Capitoline and the Palatine Hill, a marshy plain first served as a necropolis. Laid out for the first time in 616 BC or shortly after, drained by the Cloaca Maxima dug under Tarquin the Elder, the forum became the centre of ancient Rome. Left derelict from the 7th century, it served as pasture under the name Campo Vaccino.
summaries.Q659138: Planned under Julius Caesar, who cleared an area of the Campus Martius in 44 BC, the work was only taken up again in 23 BC by Augustus. The building was dedicated on 7 May 11 BC to Marcellus, his nephew and son in law. A fortress in the Middle Ages, it carries the palace Baldassare Peruzzi raised in 1532 for the Savelli, which saved it.
summaries.Q1135392: Created in 1889 to bring together the antiquities of Rome, this archaeological museum settled in the Baths of Diocletian and the monastery next to the basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri. The state bought the villa Ludovisi in 1901, whose sculptures joined it. Its works are now spread over four exhibition sites.
summaries.Q647919: Nicknamed il Cembalo, the harpsichord, because of its unusual plan, it was built between 1560 and 1614 for cardinal Camillo Borghese, the future pope Paul V. The part played by Martino Longhi the Elder and Flaminio Ponzio is debated. Its courtyard is ringed by 96 columns. It held cardinal Scipione Borghese's paintings until 1891.
summaries.Q753791: A small round temple in the Roman Forum, it held the sacred fire and the Palladium, with no statue of the goddess. Ancient authors credit the first temple to Numa Pompilius. Burnt several times, it was restored under Septimius Severus after the fire of 191. Closed in 394, it was destroyed in 1549; its ruins come from a 1930s rebuilding.
summaries.Q609293: A minor basilica of the rione Ripa, built in the 6th century in the Forum Boarium on the ruins of the Great Altar of Hercules Invictus, of which a tufa wall survives in the basement. A nearby Greek community earned it the name Schola Graeca, and its look that of Cosmedin, from the Greek Kosmidion, adorned. Its portico holds the Bocca della Verità.
summaries.Q83425: Commissioned in 1656 by pope Alexander VII from Bernini, this baroque esplanade serves as the forecourt of St Peter's Basilica. Its fourfold colonnade, 284 Doric columns and 88 pilasters, spreads out from the basilica like two arms welcoming the crowd. Bernini meant to close the square to the east: the pope's death stopped the work.
summaries.Q870476: Built by Hadrian as the Pons Aelius, at an uncertain date, it gave access to the imperial mausoleum that became Castel Sant'Angelo. The main approach to St Peter's Basilica in the Middle Ages, it was then renamed. Clement IX launched its renovation in 1667 and gave it to Bernini, who set on it ten angels bearing the instruments of the Passion.
summaries.Q185382: The largest fountain in Rome backs onto the palazzo Poli, on the piazza di Trevi. Clement XII launched a competition in 1730 to celebrate the Aqua Virgo aqueduct and chose Nicola Salvi's design; on his death in 1751, Giovanni Paolo Panini carried the work on and completed it, unveiled on 22 May 1762.
summaries.Q380530: Dedicated to Castor and Pollux, this temple in the Roman Forum was raised, according to Livy, after the vow of the dictator Aulus Postumius Albus in thanks to Castor for his part in the victory at Lake Regillus. Its podium served as a platform for orators under the Republic. Part of the base and three columns 12.5 metres high survive.
summaries.Q1136614: Urban VIII, who had bought the land from the Sforza in 1625, entrusted the building to Carlo Maderno in 1627; on his death in 1629, his nephew Borromini took over the site, at first with Bernini, who finished it alone in 1633. The Italian state acquired it in 1949 and installed the National Gallery of Ancient Art there.
summaries.Q1755046: The Senate of the Italian Republic sits there. Finished in 1505 by cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, the future Leo X, it is named after Margaret of Parma, widow of Alessandro de' Medici then wife of Ottavio Farnese. It passed to the Habsburgs, then to Benedict XIV who made it the seat of papal government, then held the senate of the kingdom of Italy.
summaries.Q738214: Constantine had it raised in the early 4th century on the presumed site of the martyrdom of Saint Lawrence. In 580 Pelagius II allowed a church to be built there; in front of the old one, Honorius III began another in the 13th century, the two structures later being joined. Bombed by the Allies in 1943, it was restored until 1948.
summaries.Q1479873: The conventual church of the Benedictine monastery next to it, in Trastevere, it is dedicated to the Roman martyr Cecilia and is said to stand on the site of her house. Paschal I had it rebuilt in 822 and brought back the saint's relics, from the catacombs of Callixtus I. The white facade was built in 1725 by Ferdinando Fuga.
summaries.Q211295: The last and most monumental of the imperial forums, it brings together the Basilica Ulpia, Trajan's Column, two libraries and Trajan's Market. Trajan funded it with the spoils of the Dacian campaigns; its construction, from 106 to 113 under Apollodorus of Damascus, required levelling the saddle between the Capitoline and the Quirinal.
summaries.Q655470: It stands at the centre of piazza Navona, in front of the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone. Bernini raised it from 1648 to 1651 for Innocent X; an unpopular tax on bread, meat and salt paid for it. Four statues stand for the Danube, the Ganges, the Nile and the Rio de la Plata, one river per continent.
summaries.Q200642: This hill, one of Rome's seven and one of the oldest parts of ancient Rome, looks onto the Roman Forum to the north and the Circus Maximus to the south. Under the Empire the emperors built imposing houses there one after another, which gave rise to the word palace. The Farnese gardens still cover the Domus Tiberiana.
summaries.Q568342: Raised at the north west end of the Roman Forum, on the slopes of the Arx, one of the two summits of the Capitoline Hill, it became at the end of the Republic the official record office of ancient Rome. Its name comes from the tabulae, the wax tablets kept there. Its upper part, renovated by Michelangelo, holds Rome's city hall.
summaries.Q1492387: Created in 1883, it first occupied the Palazzo delle Esposizioni on the via Nazionale; for the international exhibition of 1911, the government decided to put up a new museum in the villa Borghese, to plans by Cesare Bazzani. Its 55 rooms show 1,100 works, mainly Italian.
summaries.Q2047593: Built between 1644 and 1650 on piazza Navona, it has held the Brazilian embassy since 1920 and became the property of the Brazilian state in 1964. A fresco by Pietro da Cortona showing the Story of Aeneas, painted around 1651-1654, decorates the great gallery.
summaries.Q746721: One of the oldest temples built around the Roman Forum, under the Republic it held the public treasury, the Aerarium; ancient authors differ on its foundation date. Lucius Munatius Plancus began its rebuilding in 42 BC, finished towards the end of the 30s. Its eight columns probably date from the 4th century restoration.
summaries.Q1465674: The second Jesuit church of Rome in importance after the Gesù, it was begun in 1626 for the Roman College, at the initiative of cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi and to plans by Orazio Grassi. For lack of funds the planned dome was not built: Andrea Pozzo suggested it in trompe-l'oeil and painted the Apotheosis of Saint Ignatius on the nave vault.
summaries.Q463400: The largest tourist square in Rome, in the northern part of the Campus Martius, rests on the ruins of the stadium built by Domitian in 86, whose exact shape it keeps. Its ancient name, in agones, shifted into nagone, navone, then navona. The Fountain of the Four Rivers at its centre, commissioned from Bernini by Innocent X, was finished in 1651.
summaries.Q1114231: Commissioned in 1629 by pope Urban VIII from Pietro Bernini and his son Gian Lorenzo, it shows a half sunken boat taking in water on all sides, in memory of the Tiber flood of 24 December 1598, during which Romans crossed piazza di Spagna by boat. For lack of pressure it sits in a hollow at ground level.
summaries.Q189417: A Roman road over 800 km long, it starts from Rome, follows the Tyrrhenian coast and ends in Apulia. The censor Appius Claudius Caecus began the works in 312 BC: it first linked Rome to Capua, before being extended towards Taranto and Brindisi in 191 BC. The Romans called it Regina Viarum, queen of roads.
summaries.Q725404: Near the porta San Paolo, it holds the tomb of Caius Cestius, but in the Middle Ages passed for that of Remus. Built between 18 and 12 BC, 36.4 m high, it is made of concrete faced with Carrara marble slabs. Cestius's will required his heirs to raise it in 330 days, on pain of losing the inheritance.
summaries.Q2266081: Founded in 1895, this picture gallery long stayed in the palazzo Corsini; since the 1950s it has been split between the Corsini and Barberini palaces. Its collections bring together major works of Italian and European painting: La Fornarina by Raphael, Judith Beheading Holofernes and Saint John the Baptist by Caravaggio.
summaries.Q1090910: This neoclassical palace holds the Museum of Rome, which covers the city's history from the Middle Ages to the 19th century. In 1791 Pius VI had the palazzo Orsini, raised on the same spot in 1435, demolished, and Cosimo Morelli built the new one for the pope's nephew, Luigi Braschi-Onesti. Halted in 1798, the work resumed in 1802.
summaries.Q863593: A baroque church on the Via XX Settembre, rebuilt in the early 17th century to a design by Carlo Maderno and funded by cardinal Scipione Borghese to mark the Catholic victory over the Protestants at the battle of White Mountain, in Prague in 1620. It holds Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, made between 1644 and 1652.
summaries.Q1258576: Raised on the Janiculum, on the site of a 9th century church dedicated to Saint Peter, it was commissioned by Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella the Catholic and marked, at the end of the Middle Ages, the traditional place of Peter's crucifixion. Its courtyard holds the Tempietto, Bramante's small memorial temple, perhaps built as early as 1502.
summaries.Q848072: This monumental stairway climbs from piazza di Spagna to the church of Trinità dei Monti. The French diplomat Étienne Gueffier left the funds, but his will was contested and the project lay dormant until Clement XI. A competition chose Francesco De Sanctis, then almost unknown, in 1717; the steps were built from 1723 to 1725.
summaries.Q983774: Built between 1585 and 1587 by Domenico Fontana, this portico fountain carries the baptismal name of the pope who ordered it, Sixtus V, Felice Peretti. The Quirinal lacked water: the spring taken near the village of Colonna was to supply this district, the Monte Pincio and the Capitoline. Three arches shelter statues of Moses, Aaron and Gideon.
summaries.Q192784: A triumphal column in Trajan's forum, built from 107 to 113 and dedicated in May 113 by the Senate. A spiral relief unrolls along its shaft the story of the two Dacian wars, in 155 scenes. The ashes of Trajan, who died in 117, were placed in a chamber in the base. Sixtus V had a statue of Saint Peter set on top in 1587.
summaries.Q907387: The only equestrian statue of ancient Rome to have survived, 4.24 m high, it probably owes that to a mistake: it was taken for Constantine while other imperial bronzes were melted down. Paul III had it brought to the Capitoline square in 1538, where Michelangelo designed its pedestal. Restored from 1981 to 1990, it is in the Capitoline Museums.
summaries.Q1203458: A private museum of the Doria Pamphilj Landi family, in a 16th century palace between the via del Corso and the via della Gatta. Olimpia Aldobrandini brought it in 1647 to prince Camillo Pamphilj, nephew of Innocent X. The core of the collection comes from the Aldobrandini inheritance; the paintings hang in several tiers, almost without labels.
summaries.Q927092: City hall since 1144, the oldest in the world, it was raised in the 12th and 13th centuries on the ruins of the Tabularium. Paul III entrusted its renovation to Michelangelo in 1538, who regularised the facade and designed the double stair; Giacomo della Porta carried on after his death. It was the seat of the senator of Rome until 1870.
summaries.Q318660: At the top of the Capitoline Hill, the church of the Italian Senate and the Roman people is founded on the site of a Byzantine abbey recorded in 574. Given to the Benedictines, it passed to the Franciscans by papal bull in 1249-1250. A stair of 124 steps, designed in 1348, leads to it. Its Infant Jesus statue, stolen in 1994, is replaced by a copy.
summaries.Q385910: The site layers three levels: Roman buildings, including an insula with a mithraeum, a first basilica filled in after the Norman sack of 1084, and the present church, rebuilt above it by cardinal Anastasius. Father Joseph Mullooly cleared the buried basilica from 1857. Irish Dominicans have served it since 1677.
summaries.Q15124814: A pedestrian square in the historic centre, in the luxury shopping district, it took its name in 1620 when Spain set up its embassy to the Holy See there. The Barcaccia fountain, in the shape of a boat, was installed in 1629. The Spanish Steps, the work of Francesco De Sanctis, climb towards the church.
summaries.Q586329: Linking the rioni of Regola and Trastevere, it replaces an ancient bridge wanted by Agrippa, swept away by a flood in 791. Sixtus IV decided to rebuild it in 1473 and gave the work to Baccio Pontelli; open for the 1475 jubilee, it was only finished in 1479. The oculus in its central pier eases water pressure and serves as a flood marker.
summaries.Q207808: The largest and oldest circus in Rome occupies the Murcia valley, between the Palatine and the Aventine. Tradition credits its founding to Tarquin the Elder; the first permanent structures date from 329 BC, Julius Caesar enlarged it in 46 BC and Trajan rebuilt it in stone. The last race was held there in 549.
summaries.Q729490: This marble mask of the 1st century AD, 1.75 m across, shows a bearded male face with bored eyes, nose and mouth; it probably served as a drain cover. First placed outside the porch of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, it moved into the portico during the restorations ordered by Urban VIII. Its name appears in 1485.
summaries.Q1881229: A national museum of contemporary art, it came out of a project launched in 1998 by the ministry of Culture, whose architecture competition was won by Zaha Hadid. Built from 2002 to 2007 then fitted out until 2009, it opened on 30 May 2010. Its design is disputed: Hadid is reproached for favouring architectural effect.
summaries.Q1058475: Built in 1540 for cardinal Girolamo Capodiferro by Bartolomeo Baronino, it was bought in 1632 by cardinal Bernardino Spada, who had Francesco Borromini alter it. A gallery there looks 30 metres long when it is under 9 metres, through forced perspective. The Italian state bought it in 1927 for its Council of State.
summaries.Q823685: One of the few mainly Gothic churches in Rome, it was built by the Dominicans, from 1280 to 1370, on the foundations of a place of worship dedicated to Minerva. Saint Catherine of Siena and Fra Angelico are buried there. In front of the left pillar of the choir stands a Risen Christ begun by Michelangelo.
summaries.Q828143: Dedicated to the goddess Concordia, it stands at the western end of the Roman Forum. The Senate had it built or restored in 121 BC by the consul Lucius Opimius; Tiberius rebuilt it after the fire of 9 BC and filled the interior with Greek works. Almost gone, it keeps the podium foundations and the threshold of the cella.
summaries.Q824997: Laid out from the late 16th century by order of Sixtus V, it owes its neoclassical look to Giuseppe Valadier, who redrew it as two half circles between 1811 and 1823. At its centre, the Egyptian obelisk brought on Augustus's orders for the spina of the Circus Maximus was re-erected in 1589 by Domenico Fontana. Three streets fan out in a trident.
summaries.Q936296: Designed by Giacomo della Porta at the end of the Renaissance and cast in bronze by Taddeo Landini, it stands on piazza Mattei, facing the palazzo Mattei di Giove, in the ghetto. The four tortoises that give it its name are later: added during a restoration, they are attributed to Bernini or to Andrea Sacchi.
summaries.Q5786: The Roman Senate raised it to mark Constantine's victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, on 28 October 312, and his ten years in power. Unveiled on 25 July 315, the last of the series of triumphal arches in Rome, it stands out for the systematic use of pieces taken from older monuments.
summaries.Q770797: Octavian vowed a forum and a temple to Mars if he won the battle of Philippi, in 42 BC. The work probably only began between 19 and 12 BC, and the dedication of the forum, like the consecration of the still unfinished temple of Mars Ultor, took place only on 1 August of the year 2 BC.
summaries.Q338523: Gregory XIII authorised this art institution in 1577, placed under the patronage of Saint Luke, held to be the author of the first portrait of the Virgin. It really took shape in 1593 under Federico Zuccari, its first prince. After its buildings near the Roman Forum were demolished, it moved to the Palazzo Carpegna in 1934.
summaries.Q774654: Created in the 17th century by the Pamphilj, this 180 hectare park, on the Gianicolense near the porta San Pancrazio, is the largest in central Rome. The Italian state bought the central part in 1957, the city the rest in 1965 and 1971, and the whole opened to the public in 1972.
summaries.Q592244: Built on the Aventine between 422 and 432 by the priest Peter of Illyria, it is among the best preserved early Christian churches in Rome. Its 5th century cypress door is the oldest carved wood of that period: it shows a Crucifixion held to be the oldest known. Honorius III gave it to Saint Dominic in 1219.
summaries.Q576929: Ringed at the start by twenty Corinthian columns, it is the oldest monument in Rome almost entirely of marble to have survived. Its round shape long had it taken for a temple of Vesta; the 20th century recognised it as dedicated to Hercules Olivarius. It occupies the western part of the piazza della Bocca della Verità.
summaries.Q874832: An important square since ancient Rome, it takes its name from the Palazzo Venezia, which the future pope Paul II had built there in the 15th century and which was a papal residence then the seat of the Venetian republic's embassy to the Holy See. Giuseppe Sacconi gave it its present shape with the monument to Victor Emmanuel II.
summaries.Q857540: Commissioned from Gian Lorenzo Bernini by Urban VIII in 1644 for public use, it carries the bees, the heraldic emblem of the Barberini. Taken down in 1880 because it blocked traffic, it was to be put back up in 1915, but most of the pieces had gone: it is a travertine copy by Adolfo Apolloni, unveiled on 28 January 1916.
summaries.Q625149: A rampart raised around Rome as insecurity ended the Roman peace: work began in 271 under Aurelian, after the invasion of northern Italy by the Juthungi and the Vandals. Maxentius then Honorius strengthened it. Largely preserved, it marks the limit of Municipio I, the historic centre.
summaries.Q371921: The last and largest civil basilica of ancient Rome, begun by Maxentius in the early 4th century, it was finished by Constantine, victor over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Ancient basilicas had no religious function: this one held judicial business. Two earthquakes, in 847 and 1349, brought down the central nave.
summaries.Q1971299: The historic seat of the Colonna family, near piazza Venezia, it was begun in the 14th century and took five centuries to build, each period leaving its own architecture. Martin V, from the family, lived there in the 1420s. In the 17th century it became a baroque residence and the Colonna gallery, 76 metres long, was built.
summaries.Q2291560: This Renaissance building in the Vatican gardens was to serve as the pope's summer residence and a hunting lodge. Work started under Paul IV in 1558; after his death, Pius IV carried on with Pirro Ligorio and added a loggia, a gallery, a chapel, three rooms and a second floor. It houses Pontifical Academies.
summaries.Q869513: A minor basilica held by the Augustinians, on the north side of piazza del Popolo, near the gate of the same name: its position made it the first church visited by most travellers entering Rome. Sixtus IV had it entirely rebuilt between 1472 and 1477. The Cerasi chapel brings together canvases by Caravaggio and Annibale Carracci.
summaries.Q658051: Raised in the first half of the 4th century above the catacombs of the same name, it owes its byname to its position outside the Aurelian Wall. Its first dedication, Basilica Apostolorum, refers to the tradition making the catacombs a temporary burial place of Peter and Paul; the name of Saint Sebastian goes back to the 9th century.
summaries.Q28303: The name, field of flowers, is said to come from a wide meadow overlooked in the Middle Ages by the Orsini fortress. The square lies between piazza Navona and the palazzo Farnese, and holds a fruit and vegetable market every day except Sunday. At its centre stands the statue of Giordano Bruno, burnt alive there on 17 February 1600.
summaries.Q1217302: Commissioned by pope Sixtus V, these four late Renaissance fountains were built under the direction of Muzio Mattei and installed between 1588 and 1593, at the crossing of the via delle Quattro Fontane and the via del Quirinale. They stand for the Tiber, the Arno and two women taken to be Diana and Juno.
summaries.Q723887: Domitian raised it in AD 81, shortly after his brother Titus died, to mark the capture of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Second Temple. Under the vault, two reliefs show soldiers carrying off the spoils of the Temple, including the seven branched candlestick, and Titus in triumph driving a quadriga.
summaries.Q836108: Built on the Viminal from 298 under Maximian Herculius, opened in 306, they are the largest baths of ancient Rome. In 1560 the frigidarium was turned into a church: Pius IV asked Michelangelo to raise the chapel to the rank of basilica, the future Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri, and to design the charterhouse of Rome.
summaries.Q2517648: Built in the 15th century for the Riario family, in Trastevere facing the villa Farnesina, it was lived in during the 17th century by queen Christina of Sweden. Bought in 1736 by cardinal Neri Maria Corsini, it doubled in size in the rebuilding given to Ferdinando Fuga. Sold to the state in 1883, it holds the National Gallery of Ancient Art.
summaries.Q34925: The smallest of Rome's seven hills, 460 metres long, has two summits: to the north the Arx, a citadel fortified from the city's beginnings, to the south the Capitolium and its temple of Capitoline Jupiter, dedicated to the Capitoline triad. The dip between them, the Asylum, is now taken up by the Capitoline square.
summaries.Q685940: One of the seven pilgrimage churches of Rome, it is built around a room of the Sessorium palace that Helena, mother of Constantine, had turned into a chapel around 320. Tradition says it was consecrated around 325 to hold the relics of the Passion brought from the Holy Land. Its baroque look dates from Benedict XIV.
summaries.Q831361: Built in the 4th century on the via Nomentana at the request of Constantine I, this centrally planned church is the mausoleum of his daughter Constantina; another of his daughters, Helena, is buried there too. Twelve pairs of granite columns carry the drum and the dome. The ambulatory vault mosaics are very well preserved.
summaries.Q655172: The oldest and most famous street of ancient Rome, it is, with the Nova Via, the only one called via before the Empire. It links the Carinae, on the western slopes of the Oppian Hill, to the Roman Forum and the Arx. On the ides of each month priests and sacrificers carried the idulia sacra along it, which may be the source of its name.
summaries.Q1435809: Built in 1612 at the end of the aqueduct restored by Paul V, it takes its name from that pope. Giovanni Fontana and Flaminio Ponzio gave it the form of a massive gate with five arches, where five streams flow into five marble basins. Carlo Fontana added a semicircular basin for the overflow in 1690.
summaries.Q502098: Work began in 212 under Caracalla and ran to 216, the year of the opening; Elagabalus then added porticoes to the outer wall, completed later by Severus Alexander. More than eleven hectares, room for 1,600 bathers: it is today the best preserved bath building of the Roman Empire.
summaries.Q640092: The oldest stone bridge in Rome crossed the Tiber below the Tiber Island and linked the forum Boarium to Trastevere. The flood of 1598 destroyed three of its six arches, and it was not repaired: hence its name ponte Rotto. The building of the ponte Palatino carried off the two western arches in 1887; one survives.
summaries.Q2669644: A municipal museum of contemporary art near the porta Pia, on the site of the former Peroni brewery, it inherits the Galleria Comunale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea founded in 1925. Six rooms opened in September 1999, the main museum was inaugurated on 11 October 2002, and Odile Decq's extension opened to the public in autumn 2010.
summaries.Q194103: The southernmost of Rome's seven hills, between the Tiber, the Caelian and the Palatine, it stayed outside the limits of the archaic city before king Ancus Marcius joined it to them. The plebs withdrew there several times to win their rights, hence the phrase to withdraw to the Aventine. It is now a residential area.
summaries.Q638283: The French national church in Rome, between the Pantheon and piazza Navona, it was designed by Giacomo della Porta, built for the most part by Domenico Fontana, and consecrated in 1589, the year it was finished. The Contarelli chapel holds the cycle painted by Caravaggio from 1599 to 1602 on the life of Saint Matthew, in three canvases.
summaries.Q575012: On via Condotti, it was opened around 1760 by a Greek, Nicola della Maddalena, hence its name. It lines up small rooms with crimson walls covered in paintings, with marble tables and velvet armchairs. Its present look dates from 1869; it was declared a monument of historic interest in 1953.
summaries.Q958299: About 1.5 kilometres long, it runs straight from piazza Venezia to piazza del Popolo and forms the central street of the Trident district, lined with palaces and churches. The Carnival of Rome was held there; in 1874 the city ended the riderless horse race that closed it, which helped the festival disappear.
summaries.Q770949: Begun in 1886 by the architect Ennio De Rossi, it was only opened in 1911, its building having been delayed. It links the historic centre to the rione Borgo and the Vatican City, following the line of the corso Vittorio Emanuele. Three arches span 108 metres; tall plinths carry winged Victories at each end.
summaries.Q506234: Designed by Giuseppe Sacconi and built between 1885 and 1911, this white marble monument marks 50 years of Italian unification and honours Victor Emmanuel II, first king of a united Italy in 1861. Its construction destroyed a medieval quarter and was strongly contested: Romans call it the typewriter.
summaries.Q752553: This rocky ridge at the south west end of the Capitoline Hill served in antiquity as a place of capital execution: criminals were thrown from it, in particular those guilty of false witness and high treason. Its name comes from Tarpeia, who agreed to open the gates to the Sabines and was crushed under their shields.
summaries.Q145093: The residence of the popes, officially the Apostolic Palace, it grew from the restoration, begun by Nicholas V from 1447, of the old fortified palace of Eugene III. Its 55,000 m2 and about 1,400 rooms make it the largest fully inhabited palace in the world. It holds the Sistine Chapel, the Raphael Rooms and the Borgia Apartments.
summaries.Q678313: This 80 hectare municipal park grew from a vineyard turned into gardens in 1605 by Flaminio Ponzio, to plans by cardinal Scipione Borghese, around the suburban villa where he kept his art collection. The whole was finished in 1633; the present gardens, in the English style, date from the 19th century.
summaries.Q867329: The first independent work of Francesco Borromini, it takes its name from the crossroads whose four corners each carry a fountain, one built into its facade. Built for the Discalced Trinitarians between 1638 and 1641, it was consecrated only in 1646. Its small size earned it the nickname San Carlino.
summaries.Q16800590: Opened on the via Veneto on 17 January 1906, it was built by a hotel company based in Lucerne, then sold in the 1920s to the Italian chain CIGA. In 1944 it became the temporary headquarters of general Mark Clark after the American army entered Rome. La Dolce Vita was filmed around the hotel in 1960.
summaries.Q283650: The cattle market of ancient Rome, it lies along the Tiber between the Capitoline, the Palatine and the Aventine, around today's piazza della Bocca della Verità. The first bridge over the Tiber and the first river port of the city were set up there. Its temples of Portunus and Hercules Olivarius, now churches, are remarkably well preserved.
summaries.Q1759793: At the north end of piazza Navona, its basin was made in 1574 by Giacomo della Porta, who also made the Fontana del Moro, at the south end of the same square. The sculptures are much later: the Neptune, by Gregorio Zappalà, and the Nereids, by Antonio Della Bitta, date from 1878.
summaries.Q770847: Augustus had this funerary monument raised from 28 BC for himself and the imperial family, beside the via Flaminia. The mound, 87 metres in diameter, was sacked in 410, served as a fortified keep for the Colonna, as an amphitheatre from 1780, as an auditorium after the city bought it in 1907, before Mussolini's excavations.
summaries.Q622930: Begun under Caligula in 38, finished under Claudius on 1 August 52 at the same time as the Anio Novus, it takes three springs of the Anio valley and runs 68.7 km, of which 15.1 km on arches. Nero extended it after 60, the Goths damaged it in 537 during the siege of Rome. Arches survive in the Roman countryside.
summaries.Q223079: In 1574 Gregory XIII launched the building of a summer residence on a site thought healthier than the Lateran; Ottaviano Mascherino finished the first works in 1585. Enlarged by Ponzio, Maderno then Bernini, the palace was the Roman residence of thirty popes, that of the kings of Italy from 1870 to 1946, then that of the president of the Republic.
summaries.Q545404: In the rione of Ripa, 270 metres long, it occupies a ford of the Tiber that two short bridges are enough to cross: the pons Fabricius, of 62 BC, the oldest bridge in Rome still standing, and the pons Cestius, heavily reworked at the end of the 19th century. Legend has a serpent of Asclepius land there during the epidemic of 292 BC.
summaries.Q1789776: Built in the Parioli district, in the northern part of Rome, on land given by the city to the Muslim community in 1974, it was only started in 1984, to plans by Paolo Portoghesi, Vittorio Gigliotti and Sami Mousawi, and opened on 21 June 1995. The largest mosque in Europe, it holds the Italian Islamic Cultural Centre.
summaries.Q18350121: This five star hotel of 88 rooms, opened in 1845, owes its name to its popularity with British visitors. The building goes back to the middle of the 16th century, when it lodged visitors to the Palazzo Torlonia. Byron, Keats, Mark Twain and Hemingway stayed there. A renovation begun in 2008 cut the fourth floor rooms from 21 to 13.
summaries.Q1768461: These 28 white marble steps pass, by tradition, for the stair of the praetorium in Jerusalem climbed by Jesus at his trial before Pontius Pilate, and brought to Rome by Helena. The devotion, which has them climbed on the knees, is attested at the jubilee of 1450. Sixtus V had them moved in 1589 from the old Lateran palace to the Sancta sanctorum.
summaries.Q1435824: Designed in 1575 by Giacomo della Porta with a dolphin and four tritons, this double basin fountain, at the south end of piazza Navona, received in 1653 the statue of the Moor, carved by Giovanni Antonio Mari to a drawing by Gian Lorenzo Bernini. In 1874 the original statues went to the Galleria Borghese, replaced by copies.
summaries.Q265384: Raised between 176 and 192, it marks the victories of Marcus Aurelius over the Germanic Marcomanni and the Sarmatians settled north of the Danube. A hundred Roman feet high and modelled on Trajan's Column, it still stands on its original site, at the centre of the piazza Colonna that owes it its name, in front of the Palazzo Chigi.
summaries.Q2705933: Raised on the Campus Martius, on the northern edge of the Circus Flaminius, it was built between 168 and 167 BC by Cnaeus Octavius with part of the spoils of the Third Macedonian War, to mark the naval victory of Pydna over Perseus. Augustus restored it in 33 BC and placed there the standards retaken from the Dalmatians.
summaries.Q848394: The main residence of the popes from the 4th to the 14th century, it adjoins the archbasilica of St John Lateran. The Avignon papacy left it disused, and two fires did major damage. In 1586 Sixtus V had the remains of the ancient and medieval palace destroyed and charged Domenico Fontana with building a smaller one.
summaries.Q303001: A long ridge on the right bank of the Tiber, held to be the eighth hill of Rome, it is part of the rione Trastevere and reaches 85 m near the Porta Aurelia. It carries the equestrian statues of Giuseppe and Anita Garibaldi, in memory of the defence of the Roman Republic of 1849, and, at its top, a cannon set in 1904 that fires blanks at noon.
summaries.Q1137391: Among the oldest churches in Rome, it was first called titulus Callixti, after pope Callixtus I (217-222). Julius I rebuilt it on a larger scale in 340, and it was dedicated to the Virgin probably at the time of the council of Ephesus, in 431. Innocent II rebuilt it in 1140-1143, with a transept and the apse mosaics.
summaries.Q2932912: Opened in 1888 on the via del Corso, this café reached the height of its fame in the 1930s, when it became a cultural, political and social meeting place in the capital. Writers and artists gathered in the terza saletta, which Orio Vergani in 1938 called the sancta sanctorum of literature, art and journalism.
summaries.Q947037: On the Quirinal hill, straddling the rioni of Trevi and Colonna, it takes its name from the Palazzo Barberini, on its south side. At its centre stands the Triton Fountain, commissioned from Bernini by Urban VIII and dated 1642-1643. At the corner of the Via Veneto is the Fountain of the Bees: the bee is the emblem of the Barberini.
